record.original_question: For distinct digits a1, ..., an chosen from {0,1,2,...,9} with 1 < n < 9, determine how many distinct prime numbers can be formed using all of those digits, and more generally ask the same question when a1, ..., an are distinct positive integers. Also, for a fixed digit a, determine how many occurrences of a appear in the decimal expansion of the nth prime, of n!, and of n^n, and ask the analogous question for a general nonnegative integer a.

evidence.quote: How many distinct primes can we make up with all these digits? ... Let a 0 {0, 1, ..., 9}. How many digits of a does the n-th prime contain? But n! ? But nn ?

artifact.category_tag: digit statistics of primes and integer sequences
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Two related families of questions are posed.

(A) Primes from prescribed digits.
(i) Let n be an integer with 1 < n < 9, and let a_1, a_2, …, a_n be distinct digits chosen from {0, 1, 2, …, 9}. Consider all n! arrangements of these digits (those whose first digit is 0 representing the same (n−1)-digit integer). Determine, as a function of (a_1, …, a_n), the number of distinct prime numbers obtainable by concatenating all of the digits a_1, …, a_n in some order.
(ii) More generally, let a_1, a_2, …, a_n be distinct positive integers. Determine the number of distinct prime numbers obtainable by concatenating the decimal representations of a_1, …, a_n in some order (each used exactly once).

(B) Digit-count statistics.
For a fixed digit a ∈ {0, 1, …, 9} and a positive integer n, let N_a(m) denote the number of times the digit a appears in the decimal expansion of the positive integer m. Determine:
(i) N_a(p_n), where p_n is the n-th prime number;
(ii) N_a(n!);
(iii) N_a(n^n),
each as a function of n (or describe their asymptotic behavior). Pose the analogous problem when a is replaced by an arbitrary nonnegative integer, where N_a(m) is reinterpreted as the number of (possibly overlapping or non-overlapping, to be specified) occurrences of the digit string of a as a substring of the decimal expansion of m.
artifact.status_search_result: These are general-purpose questions about digit distributions in primes, factorials, and n^n, and about prime anagrams of digit multisets. No closed-form solution is known for the digit-counts of p_n, n!, or n^n in general; results exist only as asymptotic/normality conjectures and partial empirical data. Counting primes formed from a given digit multiset is a finite computational task for each instance but has no known general formula. Overall status is best classified as unknown/open.

status_evidence.title: Normal numbers and digit distribution
status_evidence.snippet: It is unknown whether n!, n^n, or the sequence of primes are normal in any base; digit distributions in these sequences are conjectural.
status_evidence.claim: Digit-count behaviour for n!, n^n, and primes is not known in closed form.
